title: Boss: on-call in vim
summary: Save a root-owned config without leaving Vim, run a macro on just the right lines, and find which file sets a setting.

steps.title: Your on-call kit
body: Three things that come up when all you have is SSH and Vim:

1. You opened a root-owned config without `sudo`, edited it, and `:w` says **E45: 'readonly' option is set** or **E212: Can't open file for writing**. `:w !sudo tee % > /dev/null` pipes the buffer to `sudo tee`, which writes the file as root. (`sudoedit` is the cleaner habit next time; Neovim does not support the `tee` trick because it cannot ask for a password there.)
2. An inventory needs the same edit on some lines but not others: `:g/pattern/norm @q`.
3. Someone's Vim indents Python by 8 and nobody knows why: `:verbose set shiftwidth?` prints the value **and the file and line that last set it**.

steps.title: E212: save it as root
prompt: `/etc/app/app.conf` is owned by root. As the learner user (not root), change `log_level = debug` to `log_level = info`, and write it **from inside Vim** with `:w !sudo tee % > /dev/null`.
The file must stay owned by `root:root` with mode `644`. After the `tee` write the buffer still counts as modified, so leave with `:q!`.

checks.name: log_level is info, nothing else changed
checks.fail: `/etc/app/app.conf` should be the same file with `log_level = info`.

checks.name: still owned by root:root with mode 644
checks.fail: Ownership or mode changed. `tee` writes into the existing file, so it keeps both; replacing the file (or `chown`) does not.

hints: `:%s/log_level = debug/log_level = info/` makes the change in the buffer.
`:w !cmd` sends the buffer to a command's input instead of writing a file. `%` is the current file name.
steps.explain: `:w !sudo tee %` saves your edit when you forgot `sudo`, without losing it. The better habit is `sudoedit /etc/app/app.conf`: your own editor and plugins run as you on a temporary copy, and only the copy back is done as root.

steps.title: A macro on just the host lines
prompt: Turn each host in `~/inventory.txt` into a two-line YAML entry, leaving the `#` comment lines alone:
(two spaces before `- host:`, four before `port:`). Put the edit in register `q` with `:let @q = "..."` and run it only on the host lines with `:g/pattern/norm @q`.

checks.name: every host is a YAML entry, comments kept
checks.fail: `~/inventory.txt` is not right yet (`<` is the goal, `>` is yours). Count the spaces.

hints: The keys for one line: `I` + `  - host: ` + Escape, then `o` + `    port: 443` + Escape.
In a `let` string: `"I  - host: \<Esc>o    port: 443\<Esc>"`. `:g/\.example\.com$/norm @q` runs it on host lines only.
steps.explain: `:g` marks the matching lines first and then runs the command on each, so the `port:` lines the macro adds are never touched themselves. That makes `:g/pattern/norm @q` safe where `5@q` would have run on the wrong lines.

steps.title: Who set shiftwidth=8?
prompt: `~/.vimrc` says `shiftwidth=4`, yet in Python files Vim indents by 8 with tabs. Find the file that sets it and fix it.

1. Ask Vim: open `~/work/sample.py` and run `:verbose set shiftwidth?`. In Ex mode the answer goes to the screen only if you redirect it: `vim -Nes -u ~/.vimrc -c 'e ~/work/sample.py' -c 'redir! > /dev/stdout' -c 'verbose set sw? et?' -c 'redir END' -c 'qa!'`.
2. Write the path of the file it names to `~/answers/culprit.txt`.
3. Fix it so Python buffers get `shiftwidth=4` and `expandtab` (remove the stale file, or correct it).

checks.name: culprit.txt names the file
checks.fail: `~/answers/culprit.txt` should hold the path `:verbose` printed after *Last set from*.

checks.name: Python buffers indent with 4 spaces
checks.fail: In `sample.py` Vim should now have `shiftwidth=4` and `expandtab`.

hints: `:verbose set sw?` prints `Last set from ~/.vim/after/ftplugin/python.vim line 2`.
Files in `~/.vim/after/` run after the normal ftplugins, so they win over your vimrc for that file type.
steps.explain: `:verbose set opt?` and `:verbose map key` answer "where did this come from?" in one line. Order matters: vimrc first, then ftplugins when a file type is detected, then `after/` files, then modelines in the file itself (if `modeline` is on).
